Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

vignette:
Priya Sharma is a 32-year-old South Asian woman who works as a registered nurse in the medical-surgical unit of a mid-sized urban hospital. She presents as composed and articulate during intake, choosing her words carefully, though she pauses frequently and looks away when the conversation turns to the events of approximately fourteen months ago. She is single, lives alone in an apartment a short drive from the hospital, and came to the current appointment, she says, because she has begun making errors at work - small ones, so far, but ones that frighten her.

The event that brought Priya to this office took place during a mass-casualty industrial incident in which a chemical plant explosion near her hospital sent dozens of critically injured workers flooding into the emergency department over the course of a single shift. Priya had been pulled from her floor to assist. What followed over the next several hours was, by any measure, extreme: inadequate protective equipment, the smell of burned skin and chemical accelerant saturating the air, colleagues making triage decisions in real time with insufficient information, patients dying before assessments could be completed. At one point Priya was alone with three patients simultaneously, all in acute distress, and she had no clear recollection of how that stretch of time resolved - only that it did, and that she was still standing at the end of her shift.

In the weeks that followed, Priya noticed something she struggled to name. The event did not settle into memory the way other difficult experiences had. Instead it existed in fragments - a pair of burned hands, a sound like something tearing, the particular quality of light in a corridor she had walked down hundreds of times before - pieces that surfaced without context or sequence and refused to cohere into a story she could hold. She found herself unable to place these images in order or connect them to one another in any way that made narrative sense, and this disorganisation unsettled her deeply. What frightened her most was not the content of any single fragment but the fact that she could not account for the whole. She had come to believe that a memory this broken must mean something was fundamentally wrong with her mind.

Compounding this was a quality she described haltingly in the second session: the sense that the event itself was simply too extreme to have been real. She would find herself thinking, with genuine uncertainty, that something of that magnitude could not have actually happened to her - to ordinary Priya, who had studied for her boards in this same city, who brought lunch from home in the same containers she had used since nursing school. The extremity of the experience seemed to place it outside the category of things that could be true, and she oscillated between this unreality and the intrusion of those disconnected sensory pieces, never quite able to hold both at once.

Over the months since the incident, Priya developed a habit of interrupting herself whenever the memory began to form more fully. She described it as a kind of internal redirection - the moment she sensed a fuller picture beginning to assemble, she would shift her attention deliberately elsewhere, to a task, to her phone, to the sounds of her apartment. She had come to regard this as practical self-management, a way of staying functional. What she had not anticipated was the cost. At work, she found that the same capacity for redirection she had trained in her private hours was now operating on the floor. She would begin a clinical handover and lose the thread mid-sentence, not from distraction but from something more effortful and harder to name - as though some part of her was pulling the information back before it fully formed. The errors she mentioned at intake had each occurred in this context: moments when the boundary between what she was deliberately not recalling and what she needed to access professionally became difficult to locate.

Priya sought help now, she said, because she could not afford to be a nurse who made errors. She had not told anyone at the hospital what she was experiencing. She was most afraid, she admitted quietly, that if she ever did allow the full memory to form, she would find something in it that confirmed her worst suspicion - that she had failed someone, and that the fragmentation itself was a kind of evidence.
